## Open-source software {#what-open-source-buys-you .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **You can read it.** The source of `lm()`, of `feols()`, of every package that this workshop loads, is public, so no estimator has to be taken on trust
- **No licence stands between a reader and your analysis.** Anyone, anywhere, can run your code without buying anything
- **It outlives your institution.** A licence expires when you change job; a package on CRAN does not
- **You can fix it, and so can others.** Bugs get found because thousands of people run the same code on different data
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
With a proprietary toolchain, **the price of reproducing your work falls on your reader**, who has to buy the licence.
:::

::: notes
Stata is proprietary and R is open source, and the difference matters for reproduction for four reasons, only one of which is money. First, you can read the source of any function that we run in this workshop, so no estimator has to be taken on trust. Second, and closest to our subject, no licence stands between a reader and your analysis, whereas a replication package that needs a licence which the reader lacks is not reproducible for that reader, however carefully it was written. Third, open-source software outlives your institution, since a site licence ends when you change job and a package on CRAN does not. Fourth, bugs get found, because thousands of people run the same code on different data. [advance] On money, the question is who pays: reproducibility has a price, and a proprietary toolchain passes it to the reader.
:::
